question: According to the Connecticut CDL Manual, the rules that tell shippers how to package hazardous materials safely and tell drivers how to load, transport, and unload them are collectively known as what?
choice_a: Containment rules
choice_b: Communication rules
choice_c: Placarding rules
choice_d: Manifest rules
explanation: Section 9.1.1 states these packaging/loading/transport/unloading rules are called "containment rules," distinct from the rules that communicate the risk covered next in the manual.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-1

question: To pass the written test for a hazardous materials endorsement, a CDL applicant must know how to do all of the following EXCEPT:
choice_a: Identify what are hazardous materials
choice_b: Safely load shipments
choice_c: Properly placard the vehicle in accordance with the rules
choice_d: Calculate IFTA fuel tax owed on the load
explanation: The manual lists identifying hazardous materials, safely loading shipments, properly placarding the vehicle, and safely transporting shipments as required knowledge areas; calculating IFTA fuel tax is not part of hazmat endorsement knowledge.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-1

question: Under the "Who Does What" framework in the Connecticut CDL Manual, which of the following is a duty of the shipper?
choice_a: Certify on the shipping paper that the shipment has been prepared according to the rules
choice_b: Refuse improper shipments
choice_c: Refuse leaking packages and shipments
choice_d: Placard the vehicle when loading, if required
explanation: The shipper packages, marks, and labels the material and certifies on the shipping paper that the shipment complies with the rules (unless pulling a carrier-supplied cargo tank); refusing improper or leaking shipments and placarding the vehicle are carrier/driver duties.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-1

question: Before transporting a shipment, what must the carrier check, per Section 9.2.2?
choice_a: That the shipper correctly described, marked, labeled, and otherwise prepared the shipment for transportation
choice_b: That the driver has a current medical certificate only
choice_c: That the shipping paper has been notarized
choice_d: That the ERG is less than one year old
explanation: Section 9.2.2 states the carrier checks, prior to transportation, that the shipper correctly described, marked, labeled, and prepared the shipment, and refuses improper shipments.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-1

question: Per Section 9.2.3, if a driver in physical control of a hazardous materials shipment is involved in an accident, what must the driver do?
choice_a: Report the accident or incident to the proper government agency
choice_b: Wait for the shipper to file the report
choice_c: Only report it if placards were displayed
choice_d: File a report only with the carrier's insurance company
explanation: The driver's duties include reporting accidents or incidents involving hazardous materials to the proper government agency when the accident occurs while the driver is in physical control of the shipment.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-1

question: According to Figure 9.1 in the Connecticut CDL Manual, how many different hazard classes exist for hazardous materials?
choice_a: Nine
choice_b: Seven
choice_c: Twelve
choice_d: Five
explanation: The manual states a material's hazard class reflects its risks and there are nine different hazard classes, shown in Figure 9.1.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-2

question: In Figure 9.1, Division 1.1 (Mass Explosion) is exemplified by which material?
choice_a: Dynamite
choice_b: Propane
choice_c: Ammonium Nitrate
choice_d: Battery Fluid
explanation: Figure 9.1 lists dynamite as the example material for Class 1, Division 1.1, Mass Explosion.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-2

question: If a diamond-shaped hazard warning label will not fit on a hazardous materials package, what does the Connecticut CDL Manual say the shipper may do?
choice_a: Put the label on a tag securely attached to the package
choice_b: Skip the label entirely
choice_c: Write the hazard class in permanent marker instead
choice_d: Use a smaller, non-standard label shape
explanation: Section 9.3.2 explains that when the diamond label won't fit, shippers may attach it on a tag securely fastened to the package, as with tags or decals used on compressed gas cylinders.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-2

question: A placarded commercial vehicle must display at least how many identical placards, and where?
choice_a: Four placards, on the front, rear, and both sides of the vehicle
choice_b: Two placards, on the front and rear only
choice_c: Three placards, on both sides and the rear
choice_d: One placard, on the front of the vehicle only
explanation: The manual states a placarded vehicle must have at least four identical placards, placed on the front, rear, and both sides so they are readable from all four directions.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-3

question: Identification numbers used to identify hazardous materials are four-digit codes preceded by which letters?
choice_a: "NA" or "UN"
choice_b: "HM" or "RQ"
choice_c: "PG" or "DOT"
choice_d: "ERG" or "CFR"
explanation: The manual states identification numbers are a four-digit code preceded by the letters "NA" or "UN," and are listed with their chemicals in the U.S. DOT Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG).
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-3

question: Before transporting a material, the Connecticut CDL Manual instructs drivers to check three main lists. Which of the following is one of them?
choice_a: Section 172.101, the Hazardous Materials Table
choice_b: The state DMV's vehicle registration list
choice_c: The National Motor Freight Classification
choice_d: The carrier's internal price list
explanation: The three lists are Section 172.101 (the Hazardous Materials Table), Appendix A (List of Hazardous Substances and Reportable Quantities), and Appendix B (List of Marine Pollutants).
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-3

question: In the Hazardous Materials Table (49 CFR 172.101), what does the entry "Forbidden" in Column 3 mean?
choice_a: The material must never be transported
choice_b: The material requires a special permit before transport
choice_c: The material may only be transported by air
choice_d: The material needs a DANGEROUS placard instead of a specific one
explanation: Column 3 shows a material's hazard class or division, or the entry "Forbidden," and the manual explicitly states a driver must never transport a "Forbidden" material.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-4

question: In Column 4 of the Hazardous Materials Table, identification numbers preceded by the letters "NA" indicate what?
choice_a: Proper shipping names used only within the United States and to/from Canada
choice_b: Names used exclusively for international air transportation
choice_c: Names recognized only by the Environmental Protection Agency
choice_d: Materials that do not require an identification number
explanation: The manual explains that "NA" is associated with proper shipping names used only within the United States and to and from Canada, while "ID" numbers are associated with names recognized by the International Civil Aviation Organization for air transport.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-4

question: In Column 7 of the Hazardous Materials Table, the numbers 1 through 6 indicate that a material is a:
choice_a: Poison inhalation hazard (PIH), with special shipping paper, marking, and placard requirements
choice_b: Marine pollutant subject to Appendix B
choice_c: Radioactive material requiring a Yellow III label
choice_d: Reportable quantity under Appendix A
explanation: The manual states that numbers 1-6 in Column 7 mean the hazardous material is a poison inhalation hazard (PIH), which carries special requirements for shipping papers, marking, and placards.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-5

question: When a hazardous substance is transported in a reportable quantity (RQ) or greater in one package, what must the shipper display?
choice_a: The letters "RQ" on the shipping paper and package
choice_b: A red "RQ" flag on the vehicle roof
choice_c: A copy of Appendix A attached to the windshield
choice_d: The word "EMERGENCY" in place of the proper shipping name
explanation: Per the Appendix A discussion, when materials are transported at or above their reportable quantity, the shipper displays the letters "RQ" on the shipping paper and package, which may appear before or after the basic description.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-5

question: If the words INHALATION HAZARD appear on a shipping paper or package, what must the driver display?
choice_a: The POISON INHALATION HAZARD or POISON GAS placard, in addition to other required placards, even for small amounts
choice_b: Only the standard hazard class placard, since inhalation hazard is already implied
choice_c: A DANGEROUS placard instead of the class-specific placard
choice_d: No placard is required if the quantity is under 1,000 pounds
explanation: The manual states the rules require display of the POISON INHALATION HAZARD or POISON GAS placard in addition to other placards required by the product's hazard class, and this applies even for small amounts since the 1,000-pound exception does not apply.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-5

question: For highway transportation, Appendix B's List of Marine Pollutants applies only to chemicals in a container with what minimum capacity, when not otherwise placarded or labeled?
choice_a: 119 gallons or more
choice_b: 55 gallons or more
choice_c: 500 gallons or more
choice_d: 30 gallons or more
explanation: The manual specifies that for highway transportation, Appendix B is only used for chemicals in a container with a capacity of 119 gallons or more without a placard or label as specified by the HMR.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-5

question: If a hazardous materials shipping paper has more than one page, what must the first page show?
choice_a: The total number of pages, for example "Page 1 of 4"
choice_b: The driver's CDL number
choice_c: The vehicle's VIN
choice_d: The carrier's DOT safety rating
explanation: The manual requires that a multi-page shipping paper's first page tell the total number of pages, using a format like "Page 1 of 4."
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-5

question: When a shipping paper lists both hazardous and non-hazardous products, how must the hazardous materials be shown?
choice_a: Entered first, and either highlighted in a contrasting color or identified by an "X" (or "RQ") in the "HM" column
choice_b: Entered last, after all non-hazardous items
choice_c: Listed on a completely separate shipping paper
choice_d: Marked only with a red asterisk, with no other requirement
explanation: Section 9.3.5 requires hazardous materials to be entered first on a mixed shipping paper and either highlighted in a contrasting color or identified by an "X" (or "RQ" for a reportable quantity) in the "HM" column.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-6

question: A signed shipper's certification is required on the shipping paper except in which situations?
choice_a: When the shipper is a private carrier transporting its own product, or when the package is provided by the carrier
choice_b: When the load is under 1,000 pounds
choice_c: When the destination is within the same state
choice_d: When the driver holds a hazardous materials endorsement
explanation: The manual states the only exceptions to the signed shipper's certification requirement are when a shipper is a private carrier transporting its own product, and when the package is provided by the carrier, such as a cargo tank.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-7

question: When required, which of the following must a shipper mark on a hazardous materials package?
choice_a: The name and address of the shipper or consignee, the shipping name and identification number, and the required labels
choice_b: The driver's name and CDL number
choice_c: The vehicle's license plate number
choice_d: The carrier's DOT number only
explanation: Section 9.3.7 lists the shipper/consignee name and address, the material's shipping name and identification number, and the required labels as items the shipper must put on the package.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-7

question: Under Placard Table 2, hazard classes (other than bulk packaging) need placards only if the total amount transported reaches what threshold?
choice_a: 1,001 pounds or more, including the package
choice_b: 500 pounds or more
choice_c: Any amount, no matter how small
choice_d: 5,000 pounds or more
explanation: The manual states that except for bulk packaging, Table 2 hazard classes need placards only if the total amount transported is 1,001 pounds or more, including the package, adding amounts from all shipping papers for Table 2 products on board.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-8

question: A driver may use a single DANGEROUS placard instead of separate placards for each Table 2 hazard class when which condition is met?
choice_a: The vehicle has 1,001 pounds or more of two or more Table 2 hazard classes, but no single class reaches 2,205 pounds or more loaded at any one place
choice_b: The vehicle carries any amount of a Table 1 material
choice_c: The shipment is entirely non-hazardous
choice_d: The driver lacks a hazardous materials endorsement
explanation: The manual explains the DANGEROUS placard is an option, not a requirement, usable when 1,001 pounds or more of two or more Table 2 hazard classes are aboard and no single Table 2 material reaches 2,205 pounds or more loaded at any one place, in which case the specific placard for that material must be used instead.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-8

question: A bulk package is defined in the Connecticut CDL Manual as a single container with a capacity greater than what amount, and must be placarded even if it only contains residue?
choice_a: 119 gallons
choice_b: 55 gallons
choice_c: 1,000 gallons
choice_d: 275 gallons
explanation: The manual defines bulk packaging as a single container with a capacity greater than 119 gallons, and states that a bulk package (and the vehicle transporting it) must be placarded even if it only has the residue of a hazardous material.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-9

question: When loading Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, what type of floor lining does the Connecticut CDL Manual require?
choice_a: A non-metallic material or non-ferrous metal lining, with tight floors
choice_b: Any lining, as long as it is fire-resistant paint
choice_c: A galvanized steel lining
choice_d: No lining is required if packages are boxed
explanation: The manual requires that when loading Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, the floor lining must be either non-metallic material or non-ferrous metal (metal without iron or iron alloys), and the floors must be tight.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-10
